title.value: Paper Decision

comment.value:
This paper introduces a labeled dataset of 62,671 brick kilns, annotated with oriented bounding boxes over 78,707 publicly available 128×128px Sentinel-2 RGB satellite images, captured between November 2023 and February 2024. The dataset addresses a pressing environmental concern of air pollution from brick kilns in South Asia, with potential impact on public health, policy, and sustainability research.

The final ratings comprise 3 × Accept (Reviewers kt9B, qXDr, 3Hht) and 1 × Borderline Accept (Reviewer GSRo). Reviewers generally find the dataset to be of high value due to its scale and the presence of manually validated labels. All reviewers agree that the benchmarking experiments are well-executed and informative. The rebuttal and discussion period were productive, with two reviewers raising their scores (3Hht: 2→5; GSRo: 3→4) based on the authors’ responses and proposed revisions, while the other two reviewers maintained their positive assessments.

It is also appreciated that the authors summarized their planned revisions clearly in the comment box. However, much of the reviewer support hinges on these commitments. If accepted, the authors are strongly encouraged to deliver on all promised updates to ensure the dataset aligns with the expectations established during the discussion phase.

Overall, the AC agrees with the reviewers that this work constitutes a valuable contribution to the community. The recommendation is to accept.

## Paper Summary
**SENTINELKILNDB** is a large-scale, hand-validated benchmark of **62,671 brick kilns** (FCBK, CFCBK, Zigzag) with oriented bounding boxes over **2.8M km²** of free **Sentinel-2 imagery**. We evaluate SOTA oriented detectors under *(i) in-region*, *(ii) cross-region*, and *(iii) super-resolution* settings, enabling the first systematic study of **continental-scale, low-resolution object detection** for environmental monitoring. The dataset offers a challenging, policy-relevant testbed for geospatial robustness.

## Rebuttal Summary
**1. Expanded Benchmarking:** Added **SatMAE ViT-Large**, **TerraMind-v1-base**, and **Galileo** with Faster R-CNN head. TerraMind and Galileo surpassed prior baselines; Galileo achieved **+14.7% recall**, **+10.4% precision**, and **+8.3 mAP@50** over RT-DETR in class-specific mode, with RT-DETR’s class-agnostic edge traced to misclassification recovery. Also reported **mAP@[50:95]**; will explore OBB heads for foundation models.

**2. Temporal & Geographic Robustness:** Four-season Lucknow analysis showed domain shifts from vegetation, atmosphere, and kiln-activity changes, validated via RGB stats on **5,184 kiln patches** (Voulgaris et al., CVPR EarthVision 2023). LOCO evaluation (India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Afghanistan) yielded CA = 46–87%, confirming dataset value for cross-region generalization.

**3. Hard Negatives & Clean Test Split:** Built **41,068** manually verified negative Sentinel-2 tiles; adding **24,842** negatives reduced FPs by **up to 97%**. Created a clean, non-overlapping test set (**10,278 images / 14,418 labels**) with stable mAP rankings, enabling robust generalization benchmarking.

**4. OBBs & Annotation Protocol:** OBBs capture rotation for ~97% of non-circular kilns, enabling MoEF&CC/CSE-compliant area estimates. High-confidence predictions average **IoU ≈ 0.75** with GT polygons. Two-stage review with dual annotators and expert adjudication ensures scalable, consistent labeling.

**5. Efficiency, Licensing & Camera-Ready:** Limited to 3 detection rounds after yield saturation (208 h for 62,062 boxes). Only Sentinel-2 imagery/annotations released; Planet imagery used for label derivation, Esri basemaps for validation only.

## Closing
We thank all reviewers and ACs for constructive feedback. The rebuttal process has strengthened the work with new experiments, analyses, and dataset resources. We respectfully request that these contributions be considered in final evaluations.

title.value: Clarification on Class Imbalance — Concern Resolved with Reviewer qXDr29

comment.value:
We thank Ethics Reviewer uBMY for flagging that Reviewer qXDr29 also raised the data imbalance issue. After our detailed explanation, **Reviewer qXDr29 was convinced** that the imbalance is not due to any dataset construction artifact. CFCBK kilns account for less than 3% of our dataset, not because of sampling bias, but because this outdated design has been largely phased out across South Asia, especially in Bangladesh, where, as the reviewer also noted, strong policy pushes have favoured cleaner kiln types like Zigzag and FCBK.

Thus, the observed class imbalance reflects the underlying ground truth rather than any artifact of dataset construction. We chose to preserve this distribution to accurately represent current brick kiln practices and support policy-relevant modeling.

That said, we acknowledge the implications this imbalance may have on generalization. As part of future work, we plan to methodologically explore strategies such as class-balanced loss functions, data augmentation, and oversampling, especially for improving performance on rare kiln types in geographically unseen regions.

title.value: Rebuttal Summary: Enhancements and Clarifications

comment.value:
We thank all reviewers for their constructive engagement. The rebuttal process led to substantial technical additions, clarifications, and dataset improvements, many of which go beyond the original scope. Below we summarize the major enhancements, their rationale, and commitments for the camera-ready version.


# Expanded Benchmarking with Remote Sensing Foundation Models


We benchmarked **SatMAE ViT-Large, TerraMind-v1-base, and Galileo** with a Faster R-CNN head, under identical settings to Table 2. All three achieved strong results; TerraMind and Galileo outperformed earlier baselines in per-class AP and mAP@50, especially for circular/fixed-chimney kilns. The result showed:

Galileo has +14.7% recall, +10.4% precision, and +8.3 mAP@50 over RT-DETR in class-specific evaluation. RT-DETR’s higher class-agnostic AP stems from recovering many misclassified predictions. We also reported mAP@[50:95] for all models and committed to exploring OBB heads for foundation models.


# Cross-Season and Cross-Country Generalization

- **Temporal:** Extended analysis to all four seasons in the Lucknow airshed, showing performance drops from vegetation/atmosphere/kiln-activity changes. RGB statistics from 5,184 kiln patches confirm spectral shifts; supported by Voulgaris et al., CVPR EarthVision 2023. We will include paired seasonal imagery and feature-space visualizations.
- **Geographic:** Performed Leave-One-Country-Out evaluation across India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Afghanistan. CA ranged 46–87%, with CFCBK consistently hard. Demonstrates the dataset’s utility for cross-region robustness.


# Reducing False Positives and Strengthening Evaluation: Negative Sampling & Clean Test Split


- **Negative Sampling:** Curated 41,068 negative Sentinel-2 tiles (8 land-cover types, manually verified).Trained models without negatives → high false positives, especially on bare vegetation (e.g., RT-DETR: 6,138 FPs). Adding 24,842 negatives in training → FPs dropped by up to 97%. We will release the negative set with metadata/scripts and negetive imagery.
- **Clean Test Split:** Implemented spatial de-duplication so no test kiln overlaps train/val. New clean split: 10,278 images / 14,418 labels. Re-evaluation showed comparable mAP@50 and consistent rankings, confirming robustness. We will release this split for generalization benchmarking.


# Accurate Area Estimation with OBBs and Structured  Annotation Protocol & Quality Control

- **Area-Aware Evaluation:** Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) capture rotation/shape for ~97% of non-circular kilns, enable consistent area estimation (MoEF&CC, CSE standards), and resolve overlaps. Area-aware analysis shows high-confidence predictions have avg. IoU ≈ 0.75 with GT polygons, validating OBB accuracy.
- **Two-stage expert-guided review:** all boxes independently checked by two annotators; ambiguous cases escalated to domain experts. Balances scalability with label consistency, following AI-TOD and Patel et al. (ACM JCSS 2025).


# Scalable Labeling, Licensing Transparency, and Camera-Ready Commitments


- **Pipeline Iterations & Efficiency:** Limited to three detection iterations due to yield saturation, cost (208 h to validate 62,062 boxes), and convergence with official kiln counts. Ensures resource-efficient scaling.
- **Imagery & Licensing Clarification:** Released only Sentinel-2 imagery and annotations. Planet imagery used under license allowing label release; Esri basemaps used only for manual validation. All final annotations aligned to Sentinel-2 to ensure full reproducibility.
- **Commitments for Camera-Ready:** Include seasonal imagery, embedding visualizations, clean test set imagery, new benchmarking model outputs, and their reproducible code.

# Conclusion
We have responded to every reviewer comment with new experiments, analyses, and planned revisions. Several reviewers explicitly noted that our responses addressed their concerns and indicated possible score increases. We hope the breadth and depth of these contributions, combined with our commitment to transparency and reproducibility, will be reflected in the final evaluation. We remain happy to address any remaining points, even post-rebuttal.

comment.value:
>*C2: Comparison between Galileo and RTDETR across class-specific and class-agnostic evaluations (AP\@50)*

We thank the reviewer for this insightful question, which led to a detailed diagnostic comparison of Galileo and RT-DETR under class-specific and class-agnostic settings (IoU ≥ 0.50).

---

### **1. Detection Efficacy – Recall (TP / G.T. Objects)**

|Model|Evaluation Mode|True Positives (TP)|Ground Truth Objects (G.T.)|Recall (%)|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|RTDETR|Class-Specific|16,737|20,896|80.1%|
|Galileo|Class-Specific|19,814|20,896|94.8%|
|RTDETR|Class-Agnostic|20,170|20,896|96.5%|
|Galileo|Class-Agnostic|20,050|20,896|95.9%|

*The class specific TP and FP numbers in the table are the sums of TPs and FPs across all classes and all images in the dataset.* 

**Interpretation**: Galileo shows a 14.7% higher recall than RT-DETR in class-specific mode, detecting 3,077 more true positives. This suggests Galileo is substantially better at correctly localizing and classifying kilns across all types. The similar class-agnostic recall suggests RT-DETR struggles more with classification than localization.

---

### **2. Detection Precision – (TP / (TP + FP))**
|Model|Evaluation Mode|True Positives (TP)|False Positives (FP)|Precision (%)|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|RTDETR|Class-Specific|16,737|97,058|14.7%|
|Galileo|Class-Specific|19,814|59,105|25.1%|
|RTDETR|Class-Agnostic|20,170|93,625|17.7%|
|Galileo|Class-Agnostic|20,050|58,869|25.4%|

**Interpretation**: Galileo's predictions are not only more complete but also more accurate. Galileo’s precision (25.1%) exceeds RT-DETR’s (14.7%) by 10.4%, confirming fewer false positives and higher reliability.

---

### **3. Transition from Class-Specific to Class-Agnostic Evaluation**
|Model|TP Gain (Agnostic–Specific)|FP Drop (Specific–Agnostic)|
|---|---|---|
|RTDETR|+3,433|3,433|
|Galileo|+236|236|

**Interpretation**:
RT-DETR gains 3,433 additional TPs when switching to class-agnostic evaluation, indicating these predictions were well-localized but misclassified. Galileo, by contrast, gains only 236 TPs, suggesting far fewer class label errors. This shows Galileo’s classification head is significantly more robust, while RT-DETR suffers from overfitting to localization and underperforms in class differentiation.

---

### **4. Class-Specific Average Precision @ IoU 0.50**


**Interpretation**:
Galileo outperforms RTDETR across all classes individually. Its class-specific mAP\@50 (73.83) is significantly higher than RTDETR’s (65.51). This performance is consistent with the higher precision and recall observed earlier.

|Class|RTDETR(AP@50)|Galileo(AP@50)|∆(Galileo−RTDETR)|
|---|---|---|---|
|CFCBK|63.43|71.34|+7.91|
|FCBK|68.74|73.08|+4.34|
|Zigzag|64.36|77.06|+12.70|
|**mAP**|**65.51**|**73.83**|**+8.32**|

---

### **5. Class-Agnostic Average Precision @ IoU 0.50**

|Model|AP@50|
|---|---|
|RTDETR|87.66|
|Galileo|84.78|


**Interpretation**: While RT-DETR achieves a higher class-agnostic AP@50 (87.66 vs. 84.78), this is largely due to recovering predictions that were previously misclassified. This confirms our earlier observation: RT-DETR localizes well but struggles to assign the correct class, leading to large drops in class-specific performance.


### **Conclusion**

To summarize:

- Galileo outperforms RT-DETR in class-specific mAP (+8.3 points), recall (+14.7%), and precision (+10.4%).
- RT-DETR's class-agnostic boost (+3,433 TPs) reveals high misclassification rates, while Galileo's smaller boost (+236 TPs) reflects superior class-label accuracy.

**Implication**: Galileo is the more balanced and reliable detector for multi-class real-world deployments, while RT-DETR's advantage lies primarily in object localization.

These results clarify why Galileo excels in class-specific mAP while RT-DETR benefits from agnostic evaluation.

---

>C2.2) Clarification on mAP@50 vs. mAP@[50:95]

We computed **mAP@50** using only a single IoU threshold of **50%**. We did **not** average precision over multiple IoU thresholds (i.e., 0.50 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05). The table below includes both **mAP@50** and **mAP@[50:95]** metrics. We will include this updated version in the camera-ready submission.

|Model|mAP@50|CFCBK@50|FCBK@50|Zigzag@50|mAP@50:95|CFCBK@50:95|FCBK@50:95|Zigzag@50:95|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|YOLO-11L-OBB|75.24|58.85|55.45|53.93|41.94|34.86|31.81|29.37|
|YOLO-Worldv2|80.75|58.08|62.29|56.92|49.91|35.20|39.94|34.40|
|RT-DETR|87.66|63.43|68.74|64.36|53.99|38.28|43.86|38.77|
|Terramind|85.37|72.75|72.45|76.86|45.37|72.25|70.72|74.81|
|Galileo|84.78|71.34|73.08|77.06|44.02|70.12|71.35|74.55|
|Satmae|81.55|53.37|59.63|65.06|39.89|49.82|57.34|62.51|

---

We hope this analysis and earlier clarifications address your remaining concerns. We greatly appreciate your thoughtful engagement, and note that other reviewers have found our responses helpful. We’d be grateful if you could consider our efforts when finalizing your evaluation.

comment.value:
>C1. For the season dynamics, the results in intra-season show huge differences. I wonder why would this happen. Do the features of a brick kiln in different seasons change a lot? I hope there will be image evidence to support this experimental result if this manuscript is accepted.


We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful follow-up.

Indeed, we observe significant performance drops during intra-season generalization (e.g., training on winter and testing on post-monsoon). These differences arise due to real-world variations in kiln appearance and surrounding context across seasons:

1. Background Variation: Vegetation, crop residue, and soil textures near kilns vary seasonally—e.g., lush fields post-monsoon vs. barren land in summer—affecting contextual cues used by detectors.

2. Illumination and Shadows: Seasonal variation in solar angle, haze, and cloud cover impacts contrast and spectral response in imagery.

3. Kiln Activity Cycles: Many kilns are seasonal and may lie dormant during non-peak months, making them harder to detect due to structural contrast.

These factors align with findings from a recent study presented at CVPR EarthVision Workshop 2023, which emphasizes:

"Domain shifts during seasonal variations are an important aspect affecting the robustness of aerial scene classification and so it is important that such variation is captured within aerial scene datasets. This is more evident in geographic locations in the global South, where aerial coverage is scarcer and the rural and semi-urban landscape varies dramatically between wet and dry seasons."
— Voulgaris et al., CVPR EarthVision 2023 [1]

Their dataset from Ghaziabad, India (also within our study region) shows similar seasonal domain shifts in rural and semi-urban settings.

To empirically support this, we analyzed 5,184 kiln-containing Sentinel-2 image patches from the Lucknow airshed. RGB channel statistics show substantial seasonal shifts:


| Season   | Mean R | Mean G | Mean B | Std R | Std G | Std B |
|----------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Winter | 76.40 | 74.68 | 63.98 | 35.31 | 31.73 | 31.10 |
| Pre-Monsoon | 89.17 | 79.77 | 69.00 | 41.85 | 35.83 | 34.78 |
| Monsoon | 96.73 | 89.76 | 79.57 | 46.66 | 42.03 | 41.17 |
| Post-Monsoon | 90.11 | 86.25 | 77.93 | 39.09 | 34.59 | 32.71 |

These differences are visually apparent and explain why domain generalization across seasons is challenging.

We agree with the reviewer that visual evidence would further clarify these findings. In the camera-ready version, we plan to include:

- Side-by-side image patches of the same kiln across different seasons.
- t-SNE (or similar) visualizations comparing deep feature embeddings by season to highlight latent domain shift. 

We note again that we can not share these presently due to NeurIPS policy. 

----


>C2. As the labels are annotated on the Planet, and authors claim Planet is able to be public, I am wondering why the reprojection of labels is needed.


Thank you for this question. While we are permitted to publicly release derived annotations (such as bounding box coordinates) from Planet imagery under their Education and Research License, we **cannot distribute the Planet imagery itself**. Consequently:

The final dataset must be aligned with publicly available imagery—specifically, Sentinel-2—so users can visualize and train models using data they can access without restriction.

Reprojection ensures label compatibility with Sentinel-2’s coordinate system and resolution (10 m/px), as PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 differ in projection, and spatial resolution.

Thus, even though the labels were initially created using Planet imagery, reprojecting them enables direct use with public Sentinel-2 images, maintaining open-access usability while respecting licensing constraints.

We will clarify this explicitly in the camera-ready version.

---

We hope this addresses your concern. Please do let us know if there are any remaining clarifications or suggestions—we would be grateful for your continued consideration in improving the evaluation and final score.

title.value: Response to Reviewer 3Hht: Clean Split Evaluation, Area-Aware Metrics, and Clarifications on mAP@50 Behavior

comment.value:
We continue our response to the reviewer here. 

---

> C6) Overlap between splits
I am concerned by the significant overlap in kilns between the splits. From personal experience on curating several satellite imagery-based benchmarks, models tend to be very capable of memorizing objects even if they are translated in an image. Is there any way that the authors could separate out a clean test set that does not feature any overlaps with the train and val splits? Also, what does it mean for the test set to have 21,100 labels yet it has 34,652 overlapping kilns? I understand that some images may feature multiple kilns. Still, this seems like an exceptionally high overlap rate. ----> give result of trained models on reduced test set which contains no overlapping images.

### Creation of a Clean, Non-Overlapping Test Set

We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern. In response, we have implemented a spatial de-duplication procedure to construct a clean test split where no test kiln has any spatial overlap with any train or validation kiln—even partially.

### Dataset Stats Before and After Filtering

| Split Type               | Original Test Set | Clean Test Set (No Overlap with Train/Val) |
|--------------------------|------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|
| No. of images            | 15,739            | 10,278|
| Unique kilns             | 12,515            | 11,170 |
| Label instances          | 21,100            | 14,418  |

The drop in image and instance count reflects the strict exclusion of overlapping objects.


### Model Performance on Clean Test Set

We re-evaluated all benchmark models on the clean test split. Results below show that models perform comparable to the original split.

| Model            | mAP@50 (Original) | mAP@50 (Clean) | CFCBK@50 (Original) | CFCBK@50 (Clean) | FCBK@50 (original | FCBK@50 (Clean) | Zigzag@50 (Original) | Zigzag@50 (Clean) |
|------------------|--------------|--------------|---------------|----------------|--------------|---------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| YOLOv11L-OBB     | 75.20        | 75.24        | 58.57         | 58.85          | 55.43        | 55.45         | 53.90           | 53.93           |
| YOLO-Worldv2     | 80.74        | 80.75        | 57.78         | 58.08          | 61.28        | 62.29         | 56.89           | 56.92           |
| RT-DETR          | 87.53        | 87.66        | 63.03         | 63.43          | 68.60        | 68.74         | 64.30           | 64.36           |





As we continue refining the dataset and responding to reviewer suggestions, we plan to:

- **Release this clean test set** alongside the main dataset, clearly marked for **generalization benchmarking**.
- **Include hard negative images** during training to further improve robustness.


We hope this addresses your concern effectively, and we **sincerely appreciate your push** toward making our benchmark **more rigorous and realistic**.



---


> C3) Area metric
Now that I am more convinced that OBBs are good enough for actually calculating kiln area (see (A2) above), I’d like to see a performance metric that accounts for area. Could you please report some area-specific performance metric? For example, a plot of model confidence vs. overall IoU would be very cool to see.


We thank the reviewer for this excellent suggestion. In response, we evaluated an area-aware metric by analyzing the relationship between model confidence and polygonal IoU (intersection-over-union of oriented bounding boxes) across all matched predictions (IoU > 0.1).

We grouped predictions into confidence bins and report summary statistics below:

| Confidence Bin | Count | Avg IoU  | Min IoU  | Max IoU  |

We thank the reviewer for their sustained engagement and constructive discussions throughout the review process, as well as their openness to consider increasing the score. We believe these have helped us improve the paper substantially. We are continuing to address key concerns raised.

---

>C1) Foundation models clarification
Could you please clarify whether the foundation models mAP values are for predict oriented (OBB) vs. axis-aligned (AA) bounding boxes?


We thank the reviewer for this important question. The mAP@50 values reported for SatMAE, TerraMind-v1-base, and Galileo correspond to axis-aligned (AA) bounding boxes. These foundation models were evaluated using the default Faster R-CNN detection head from Torchvision, which does not support oriented bounding boxes.

We will clarify this in the camera-ready version. While we have not yet adapted these models to produce OBB predictions, we agree this is a promising direction and are exploring it.

---

> C4) Image count inconsistencies
Could you please resolve several inconsistencies in the image counts? Table 1 shows 78,707 total images, your Kaggle page lists 78,694 images, and your rebuttal writes 78,693 images.


Thank you for catching this inconsistency. The correct and final image counts are:

- Train: 47,215
- Validation: 15,739
- Test: 15,739
- **Total**: 78,693

The discrepancy was due to a minor human oversight during proofreading. We apologize for the confusion and will ensure the correct number is used consistently in the camera-ready version and associated dataset documentation.

---

>C5.Negative set
The rebuttal mentions that the authors have curated a new set of 41,068 negative Sentinel-2 tiles. Were any of the models trained on these negative images? If so, what is the false positive rate of the various models on this set? 

We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. We conducted two sets of experiments to measure model behavior on the newly curated negative image set.




### E1: Models Trained Only on Positive Images, Tested on Negatives

We trained all models on the original 47,215 positive images (as per Table 2 in the main paper) and evaluated them on 41,068 curated negative Sentinel-2 tiles.

Thank you for your follow-up and for the opportunity to clarify this important point regarding imagery and annotation licensing.

---

### TL;DR:
- We **only release Sentinel-2 imagery** and corresponding annotations. 
- **Planet imagery** was used for model training and annotation bootstrapping, as permitted under their **Education and Research license**. 
- **Esri imagery** was used **only for manual verification** and not for training. 
- There is **no redistribution or dependency on Planet imagery** in the final dataset.

---

### Detailed Clarification

1. **Planet Imagery — Used for Training, Not Released** 
We began with 30,638 kiln annotations from prior work based on Planet imagery under Planet’s [Education and Research License](https://www.planet.com/education/). This license:
   - Allows model training using Planet imagery.
   - Allows release of **derived products**, including geospatial annotations such as bounding boxes, centroids, or polygons.
   - **Does not allow** sharing the original Planet imagery.

Thus, we trained our YOLOv11L-OBB model on Planet imagery, but we do **not release** any Planet pixels. The only derived content from Planet use are the bounding box coordinates (e.g., geo-registered annotations), which the license explicitly permits for public academic use.

2. **Esri Imagery — Used for Validation Only** 
To validate model predictions, we used high-resolution Esri Wayback imagery **manually** for visual inspection. 
Due to its licensing restrictions:
   - We do **not** use Esri imagery for model training.
   - We do **not** redistribute Esri imagery.
   - It was only used in-browser as a human-verification layer.

3. **Sentinel-2 Imagery — Used in Final Release** 
All final annotations are **manually validated and re-aligned** to Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m/px), which is **publicly available and redistributable**. 
The released dataset consists of:
   - Sentinel-2 image tiles 
   - Corresponding geo-aligned OBB annotations 
   - Metadata for reproducibility. 
   There is **no requirement for Planet access** to use or reproduce results from our public release.

---

### Summary

| Imagery Source | Purpose                     | Used for Training | Used for Validation | Released in Dataset | Licensing Status                           |
|----------------|-----------------------------|-------------------|---------------------|----------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Planet**     | Bootstrapping + Training     | Yes               | No                  | No                   | Derived labels allowed; imagery not allowed |
| **Esri**       | Manual validation (visual)   | No                | Yes                 | No                   | Not licensed for training or redistribution |
| **Sentinel-2** | Final dataset alignment      | Yes (final models)| Yes                 | Yes                  | Public and redistributable                  |

---

We hope this clarifies the confusion. We will include this explanation in the **camera-ready version** to ensure clarity for all users. Thank you again for your engagement and attention to detail.

I thank the authors for a thorough rebuttal to my original review. I particularly appreciated the following:

A1) I appreciate the added comparison with foundation models. As I suspected, the latest earth-observation foundation models (especially TerraMind and Galilieo) perform very well.

A2) I appreciate the additional justification for using oriented bounding boxes (OBBs). In particular, the fact that the circular kilns (CFCBK) make up only ~3% of actual modern kilns alleviates my concern about the OBBs not sufficiently capturing the area of kilns. This important fact needs to be added to the camera ready if the paper is accepted.

A3) I appreciate the clarification about the dataset creation process and the distinction between PlanetScope vs. ESRI images. I also appreciate the detailed information about the 3 iterations of the detection pipeline. Please include this information in the camera ready if the paper is accepted.

A4) I appreciate the authors clarifying the issue of overlapping tiles between the train, validation, and test splits. This, however, raises new issues -- see below.

A5) I appreciate the authors cite and discuss SustainBench, as well as improve their writing.

Based on the authors’ rebuttal, I am inclined to increase my score from 2 (reject) to 3 (borderline reject). I am willing to further raise my score further if the following concerns are addressed:

**C1) Foundation models clarification**

Could you please clarify whether the foundation models mAP values are for predict oriented (OBB) vs. axis-aligned (AA) bounding boxes?

**C2) mAP@50 clarification**

Could you please help me understand how TerraMind-v1-base and Galileo achieve the best class-specific mAP@50 values across all classes, yet they have worse class-agnostic mAP@50 than RTDETR?

Also, could you please clarify whether you compute mAP@50 using only the single IoU >= 50% threshold, or are you further averaging precision over multiple IoU thresholds 0.50, 0.55, …, 0.90, 0.95?

**C3) Area metric**

Now that I am more convinced that OBBs are good enough for actually calculating kiln area (see (A2) above), I’d like to see a performance metric that accounts for area. Could you please report some area-specific performance metric? For example, a plot of model confidence vs. overall IoU would be very cool to see.

**C4) Image count inconsistencies**

Could you please resolve several inconsistencies in the image counts? Table 1 shows 78,707 total images, your Kaggle page lists 78,694 images, and your rebuttal writes 78,693 images.

**C5) Negative set**

The rebuttal mentions that the authors have curated a new set of 41,068 negative Sentinel-2 tiles. Were any of the models trained on these negative images? If so, what is the false positive rate of the various models on this set?

**C6) Overlap between splits**

I am concerned by the significant overlap in kilns between the splits. From personal experience on curating several satellite imagery-based benchmarks, models tend to be very capable of memorizing objects even if they are translated in an image. Is there any way that the authors could separate out a clean test set that does not feature any overlaps with the train and val splits?

Also, what does it mean for the test set to have 21,100 labels yet it has 34,652 overlapping kilns? I understand that some images may feature multiple kilns. Still, this seems like an exceptionally high overlap rate.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful feedback and for recognizing the strengths of our submission, particularly the benchmarking of multiple state-of-the-art detectors and the creation of a large-scale OBB dataset for brick kiln detection. Below, we respond to the concerns raised.


## Label quality and manual validation effectiveness
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the reliance on model predictions during label generation. To clarify, the initial set of 30,638 kilns from prior work served as a seed for three rounds of human-in-the-loop expansion, where each model prediction was manually verified using high-resolution imagery.

To quantify the value of this process, 
- $M_0~K$ : Kilns reported in prior study [1] (baseline count) 
- $M_i~\text{NPP}$ : Newly predicted positives by model in pass $i$ 
- $\Delta M_i~K$ : Kilns newly confirmed via manual validation in pass $i$ 
- $M_i^K$: Cumulative confirmed kilns after pass $i$: $M_iK = M_{i-1}K + \Delta M_iK$
- $M_0~K$ : Kilns reported in prior study [2] (baseline count) 
- $M_i^T$: Manual validation time in pass $i$; $\propto M_i{\text{NPP}}$


| Country     | $M_0~K$ | $M_1~\text{NPP}$ | $\Delta M_1~K$ | $M_2~\text{NPP}$ | $\Delta M_2~K$ | $M_3~\text{NPP}$ | $\Delta M_3~K$ | $M_1~T$  | $M_2~T$  | $M_3~T$  | $M_3~K$ | Total $T$ |
|-------------|---------|------------------|--------|------------------|----------------|------------------|----------------|----------|----------|----------|---------|------------|
| India       | 30,638  | 8,799|7,105|6,542|2,985|8,554|2,254|27h 17m|35h 38m|9h 23m|42,982|99h 3m|
| Bangladesh|0|6,399|6,200|599|296|692| 407| 26h 40m  | 2h 30m   | 2h 10m   | 6,903   | 31h 20m    |
| Pakistan|0|8,786| 8,051|3,334|1,417          | 6,534 | 2,709          | 36h 37m  | 13h 57m  | 27h 13m  | 12,177  | 77h 47m    |
| **Overall** |30,638| 23,984| 21,356  | 10,475           | 4,698          | 15,780           | 5,370          | --       | --       | --       | 62,062  | 208h 10m   |

This structured process reflects the high confidence and rigor with which our dataset was constructed.

[1] Patel et al., *Space to Policy: Scalable Brick Kiln Detection*, ACM JCSS, 2025.


## Visual comparison and representative results

We agree that representative visualizations can offer additional insight and fully intend to include them in the camera-ready version. Due to NeurIPS policy:

> “We prohibit use of any links in the rebuttal (including but not limited to anonymous or non-anonymous URL links), or updating your submitted data or code repositories,”

## Justification for using oriented bounding boxes (OBBs)
We thank the reviewer for raising this point and agree to tone down our claim in the camera-ready. We now clarify our rationale below:

**1. Balancing annotation cost and spatial precision:**
While pixel-wise masks are more precise, they are prohibitively time-consuming for 62K+ kilns across multiple countries. OBBs offer an effective trade-off: they approximate kiln shape and orientation while being far faster to annotate.

**2. Relevance of area estimation:**
For ~97% of kilns (non-circular), OBBs enable consistent estimates of kiln footprint area. Domain knowledge and regulatory standards confirm that kiln area is a strong proxy for production capacity, which directly influences emissions. Specifically:

The 2009 MoEF&CC emission standards categorize Bull’s Trench Kilns into small, medium, and large production capacities based on trench width (which scales with area) [1].

The CSE Zigzag Kiln Design Manual [2] further quantifies output as a function of kiln area. These public references demonstrate that kiln area is already used to classify capacity and can inform:

- Regulatory targeting: Identify kilns exceeding permitted production levels (Consent to Operate).

- Emission modeling: Move beyond average assumptions to area-informed emissions per kiln.

**3. Preserving orientation and structure:**
Kilns are elongated and densely clustered, often aligned at arbitrary angles. OBBs capture their true geometry and orientation which is crucial for distinguishing kiln types and resolving overlaps. Axis-aligned boxes lose this structural detail.

**4. Alignment with remote-sensing benchmarks:**
Leading benchmarks like DOTA-v2.0, and AI-TOD-v2 adopt OBBs to capture rotated man-made structures. Our use of OBBs ensures compatibility with these detectors and evaluation tools.

summary.value: The authors release SENTINELKILNDB, the first large-scale brick-kiln detection dataset built from free Sentinel-2 imagery (10 m GSD) with oriented bounding-box (OBB) annotations. Spanning ~2.8 M km² across India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, the dataset contains 62 671 kilns (Zigzag, FCBK, CFCBK) and >78 k image chips. Labels were generated via an iterative “Planet-based prediction → manual verification → transfer to Sentinel-2” workflow. All data and code are open-sourced under CC BY-NC 4.0 / MIT. limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The current dataset is restricted to a narrow temporal window (November 2023 to February 2024), corresponding to the peak brick kiln activity during the winter season. While this choice ensures high contrast and better visibility of kilns, it limits the dataset’s applicability for year-round monitoring, trend analysis, or studying the seasonal dynamics of kiln operations.
2. The dataset relies on initial predictions from a Planet-based model to guide the brick kiln detection pipeline, followed by manual validation. While efficient, this approach may introduce sampling bias by missing kilns that were not detected in the initial pass (false negatives) or by including incorrectly predicted ones (false positives). Additionally, the dataset exhibits a pronounced class imbalance (e.g., only ~3% of kilns are CFCBK while Zigzag kilns make up 42%), which could affect downstream model performance and fairness. 
3. This paper does not report any confidence scores or inter-annotator agreement metrics to quantify the uncertainty of the manual labeling process.
4. The current evaluation focuses on in-region vs. out-of-region generalization using a few areas. However, a more rigorous assessment of geographic robustness would benefit from a leave-one-country-out (LOCO) validation setting, given the dataset spans multiple countries with distinct kiln characteristics.

summary.value:
Small, unregulated brick kilns are a major source of pollution in South and Southeast Asia, but detecting them manually (either through ground surveys or satellite imagery) is time consuming and expensive. The SentinelKilnDB provides a labeled dataset of 62,671 brick kilns, annotated by oriented bounding boxes across 78,707 publicly and freely accessible 128x128px RGB images from the Sentinel-2 satellite, taken between November 2023 and February 2024. The labeled dataset is constructed in the following way:

1. Starting with 30,638 known labels from prior research
    
2. Train a YOLOv11L-OBB model to predict the known labels using cloud-free Planet Labs imagery (4.77m/px) from Q1 2024.
    
3. Run the trained model on (presumably) Planet Labs imagery covering a much larger area of South Asia.
    
4. Manually validate each prediction from the YOLOv11L-OBB model based on high-res Esri Wayback imagery (30cm/px).
    
5. Append the manually-validated labels to the set of known labels.
    
6. Repeat steps 2-5 for 3 times.
    

The authors perform 3 experimental analyses based on SentinelKilnDB.

1. The authors compare the mAP50 performance of 18 different models on a class-wise stratified 60:20:20 split of the dataset, showing that transformer-based models tend to perform better than one-stage or two-stage methods.
    
2. The authors compare mAP50 performance of 5 different models in an out-of-distribution task. The models are trained only on images from Uttar Pradesh, and tested on Dhaka and Punjab locations. The transformer-based model performs the best overall.
    
3. The authors test the performance gain from applying super-resolution to the input satellite imagery for a YOLOv11L-OBB model. The results show substantial performance improvement, even with simple bilinear interpolation.

strengths_contributions.value:
**SC1) Large set of manually validated labels**

To the best of my knowledge, this is the largest set to date of manually-validated labels for imagery of brick kiln.

**SC2) Experiments provide clear directions for future research**

The experiments demonstrate a steep decrease in performance in out-of-distribution settings, and a significant increase in performance with super-resolved initial images.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**LW1) Insufficient justification for why oriented bounding box (OBB) annotations the preferred label type**

While I applaud the authors for their efforts to manually curate tens of thousands of labels, I hope the authors can better justify why OBB annotations are the appropriate label for the downstream tasks suggested in the introduction: kiln identification and kiln area estimation.

On lines 80-82, the authors suggest that OBB annotations are helpful “for precise estimation of kiln area.” To me, it would seem that pixel-level segmentation masks would be a more precise annotation format for estimating kiln area. Figure 3(a), for example, illustrates how OBBs are not particularly well-suited for capturing the area of the circular kilns (CFCBKs).

On the other hand, if the goal is to merely detect kilns, then classification methods such as those used by Lee et al. (reference [25] in the manuscript) should suffice.

And if the goal is to count the number of kilns and/or geolocate kilns, then axis-aligned bounding boxes would also seem sufficient to me.

To address this concern of mine, I think that the authors could do either (or both) of the following:

- Provide stronger justification for why OBB annotations are particularly well-suited for downstream tasks
    
- Limit or remove the claims in the paper for why OBB annotations are superior to other forms of annotations
    

**LW2) Lack of clarity about dataset creation process**

I have several concerns related to the lack of clarity about the dataset creation process.

a. What exactly was the dataset used to train the YOLOv11L-OBB model for predicting labels? I’m guessing this was the Planet Labs imagery, but the paper does not make this clear.

b. Why use Planet Labs imagery at all? It seems that the justification for using Planet Labs imagery is that it has higher resolution than Sentinel-2. However, the authors also seem to have access to ESRI Wayback Imagery which is much higher resolution than Planet Labs. Why not train the YOLOv11L-OBB model on ESRI imagery?

c. Why stop at 3 iterations of the brick kiln detection pipeline? Were there time / cost constraints? Did the number of new kilns found at each round decrease? And if so, by how much?

**LW3) How does the dataset handle images without kilns?**

Table 1 suggests that there are more images than labeled kilns, which means that there should be some images that don’t have any labeled kilns. On the other hand, the dataset’s Kaggle page says “78,694 images (each with at least one kiln instance)”. Does this mean that some kilns show up in multiple images? If so, how do the authors ensure that there is no contamination between train/val/test splits? And if there are no negative images (i.e., images containing no kilns), how can the dataset accurately evaluate the false positive rate of different models?

If the dataset does contain images without any labeled kilns, how were these images chosen? What is the distribution of these images? Are these images manually validated to not have kilns?

**LW4) Lack of comparison with remote sensing foundation models**

With the growing popularity of earth-observation foundation models (e.g., newer models like Galileo, TerraMind, or Clay, and older ones like Sat-MAE), it is only useful to train specialized object detection models if the existing foundation models perform poorly. Therefore, I believe it is necessary for the authors to benchmark at least a couple of these off-the-shelf foundation models on the kiln detection task.

**LW5) Missing SustainBench reference**

The paper is missing a reference and discussion about SustainBench, which has a brick kiln remote sensing dataset and detection task.

**LW6) Lack of clarity and conciseness in writing**

- Frequent repetition. For example, the 2.8 million km2 region is mentioned 5 times in the paper (including in the abstract). Likewise, the 30,638 pre-existing labels are mentioned 4 times.
    
- Poor formatting: e.g. table captions should go on top of tables, not below tables
    
- Lines 275-276: “For task T2, we use” is repeated twice
    
- Why does the paragraph starting on line 57 give two different references for Planet Imagery?
    
- What does “accelerate accuracy” mean in line 238?

additional_feedback.value:
A1) Figure 3 seems to be reproduced exactly from the authors’ previous paper, *Space to Policy*. The authors should make it clear that Figure 3 is a reproduction of an existing figure, and not a “new” contribution.

A2) The authors seem to use a YOLOv11L-OBB model for both the dataset creation process, as well as benchmarking. For dataset creation, my understanding is that the model is trained on Planet imagery. For results reported in Tables 2 and 3, is that exact same model (trained on Planet imagery) used on the SentinelKilnDB’s Sentinel-2 imagery? Or is the model re-trained on Sentinel-2 imagery?

A3) Typos:

- Table 3: should say “ConvNeXt” instead of “ConvNet”
    
- Figure 10: should say “Bilinear” instead of “linear”

final_justification.value:
I raised my score from 2 to 3 after the rebuttal, which addresses several key questions from my original review. However, the rebuttal also raised additional concerns.

The authors then satisfactorily addressed my concerns from the rebuttal, and they have also addressed the concerns from other reviewers, so I now recommend the paper for acceptance, bumping up the score from 3 to 5 (accept).

summary.value: This paper introduces SentinelKilnDB, a large-scale, hand-validated dataset for oriented object detection of brick kilns across South Asia using freely available Sentinel-2 satellite imagery. The dataset includes 62,671 brick kilns across India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, annotated with oriented bounding boxes (OBBs). The authors benchmark 18 state-of-the-art object detection models, including transformer-based and YOLO variants, across in-region, out-of-region, and super-resolution tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Significance and Impact: The dataset targets a critical environmental issue (air pollution in South Asia), tied to public health, policy, and sustainability.
2. Scale and Coverage: One of the largest open datasets for oriented object detection in low-resolution remote sensing and the largest for Kiln Detection (62,671 annotated kilns across 2.8 million km²).
3. Manually validated labels
4. Strong Benchmarks: Evaluation includes 18 diverse models across multiple paradigms (e.g., YOLO, RoI Transformer, RT-DETR) with meaningful ablation on geographic generalization and super-resolution.
5. Discussion on super resolution impact and extension as a benchmark for OBB models, not just for Kiln detection.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The authors' argument for OBB vs bounding boxes is "[...] critical 52 for downstream tasks such as estimating production capacity and emission factors." which is neither explained nor cited. Additional clarity on why this is truly better than bounding boxes (which is easier to annotate and more vastly used) would benefit the quality of the paper.
2. The authors mention their previous work and on detecting 30,638 brick kilns using Planet imagery and the fact that the data could not be released to to Planet Lab's policy. They then proceed to integrate this data into their current dataset without explaining how that policy affects it. Why is it still not covered by Planet Lab's policy?
3. Class Imbalance Issues: Some kiln classes (e.g., CFCBK) are underrepresented, and distribution of Kiln types varies significantly (e.g., Bangladesh has more Zigzag kilns due to policy pushes). This can lead to poor generalization in out-of-region settings. Strategies for mitigating this imbalance ( weighting, oversampling) are not discussed.
4. Super-Resolution Analysis: The super-resolution adaptation task is promising but lacks detailed discussion on the methods used or their practical implications. For example, the paper could clarify which super-resolution algorithms were tested and how they impact computational cost or deployment feasibility.

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: Please clarify the situation regarding planet lab's policy on the previous work that is included in the current dataset.

dataset_code_comments.value: Github contains information on how to run and reproduce the code using MMRotate, Ultralytics, RFDETR and DETA.

final_justification.value: The authors addressed my concerns and have provided an overall good rebuttal. I will maintain my initial rating.

title.value: SentinelKilnDB: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for OBB Brick Kiln Detection in South Asia Using Satellite Imagery

TLDR.value: We propose a large-scale brick kiln dataset and benchmark using satellite imagery.

abstract.value:
Air pollution was responsible for 2.6 million deaths across South Asia in 2021 alone, with brick manufacturing contributing significantly to this burden. In particular, the Indo-Gangetic Plain; a densely populated and highly polluted region spanning northern India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and parts of Afghanistan sees brick kilns contributing 8–14% of ambient air pollution. Traditional monitoring approaches, such as field surveys and manual annotation using tools like Google Earth Pro, are time and labor-intensive. Prior ML-based efforts for automated detection have relied on costly high-resolution commercial imagery and non-public datasets, limiting reproducibility and scalability. In this work, we introduce SENTINELKILNDB, a publicly available, hand-validated benchmark of 62,671 brick kilns spanning three kiln types Fixed Chimney Bull’s Trench Kiln (FCBK), Circular FCBK (CFCBK), and Zigzag kilns - annotated with oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) across 2.8 million km2 using free and globally accessible Sentinel-2 imagery. We benchmark state-of-the-art oriented object detection models and evaluate generalization across in-region, out-of-region, and super-resolution settings. SENTINELKILNDB enables rigorous evaluation of geospatial generalization and robustness for low-resolution object detection, and provides a new testbed for ML models addressing real-world environmental and remote sensing challenges at a continental scale. Datasets and code are available in SentinelKilnDB Dataset and SentinelKilnDB Bench-
mark, under the Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International License.
